tldr: This research dramatically suppresses walking drift and turning biases in humanoids carrying one-handed loads by combining reflection-consistent feature modulation conditioned on disturbance wrenches (forces and moments) with cross-load tracking consistency training.
hero_caption: The overall framework of ReACT. The disturbance estimator on the left predicts external wrenches, modulates actor features while preserving reflection symmetry (top-center), and reinforces learning using consistency rewards (bottom-right) that penalize response discrepancies across unloaded, left-loaded, and right-loaded conditions under identical commands.
overview:
Carrying objects with humanoid robots is a crucial challenge for practical deployment in warehouses and homes. However, carrying a heavy object in one hand introduces a persistent asymmetric upper-body load. Because bipedal robots alternate their stance leg with every step, this persistent asymmetric load causes accumulated velocity tracking biases—such as sideways drift or heading deviations—even without causing the robot to fall. These accumulated errors lead to collisions with walls and obstacles during navigation.

To solve this, the authors propose "ReACT," a framework that maintains accurate velocity tracking even under asymmetric loads. The framework focuses on two key ideas. First, "reflection-consistent disturbance modulation" reflects disturbance forces and torques into the policy's features while strictly preserving the bilateral (reflection) symmetry of the robot's body. Second, "cross-load tracking consistency training" runs three parallel environments during training—unloaded, left-hand loaded, and right-hand loaded—and directly penalizes discrepancies in linear displacement and yaw rotation under the same velocity command.

Evaluations in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid show that ReACT drastically reduces lateral and yaw tracking errors compared to FALCON, a leading baseline method. Furthermore, in real-world mapless autonomous navigation experiments under a unilateral 1.5 kg hand load, ReACT achieved collision-free goal reaching in 100% of the 40 tested trials.
contributions: Proposed a reflection-consistent disturbance modulation mechanism that strictly preserves action symmetry under bilateral reflections while accounting for external disturbance wrenches (forces and moments).

Introduced cross-load tracking consistency training, directly aligning displacement and heading responses across unloaded, left-hand loaded, and right-hand loaded conditions under identical velocity commands.
Demonstrated 100% collision-free goal reaching across all 40 navigation trials in unknown real-world environments on a physical Unitree G1 carrying a unilateral 1.5 kg load.

sections.heading: Why do humanoids drift when carrying a load in one hand?
sections.summary: When a humanoid carries an object in one hand, persistent asymmetric upper-body loads introduce persistent lateral drift and yaw biases during locomotion. Because these errors accumulate and heighten collision risks, this paper proposes ReACT, unifying disturbance modulation and cross-load consistency training.
sections.details:
Recent humanoid robots have advanced to complex tasks such as whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport. A fundamental requirement for these transport tasks is accurately tracking velocity commands (linear and turning velocities) dispatched by high-level navigation policies.

However, unlike statically stable mobile bases, bipedal humanoids switch their stance leg back and forth with each step. In common real-world scenarios such as carrying an object in one hand, persistent asymmetric loads act on the upper body. Even if the robot stays stable and avoids falling, this introduces small but persistent lateral velocity biases and yaw rate deviations. Over time, these minor tracking biases accumulate into large position and heading errors, causing the robot to collide with walls and obstacles during navigation.

Conventional domain randomization (training across randomly perturbed environmental parameters) and adversarial disturbance training often improve robustness at the expense of tracking accuracy. Meanwhile, approaches like ADAPT that estimate external disturbances and feed them into the policy still struggle with remaining lateral drift under heavy unilateral loads.

To address this challenge, the authors introduce "ReACT," a new framework combining reflection-consistent disturbance modulation with cross-load consistency training, demonstrating its effectiveness on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

sections.heading: How to reconcile disturbance adaptation with morphological symmetry
sections.summary: Existing load-resilient locomotion relies on domain randomization, history-based adaptation, and disturbance observers, but struggled to completely eliminate persistent tracking biases. While reinforcement learning frameworks incorporating morphological symmetry exist, symmetry alone does not eliminate load-dependent tracking deviations; thus, ReACT introduces disturbance modulation and cross-load comparisons.
sections.details:
### II-A Humanoid Locomotion under External Loads
Initial approaches to stabilize walking under disturbances used domain randomization and adversarial disturbance training. However, expanding randomization ranges excessively degrades tracking precision. In response, history-based methods like RMA and A-RMA emerged to infer environmental latents from proprioceptive history, while FALCON adopted curriculum learning to coordinate the upper and lower body.

Methods utilizing explicit disturbance feedback have also been explored, such as MOB-Net, which estimates disturbance torques without dedicated sensors, and ADAPT, which supplies analytical disturbance estimates to the policy. ReACT shares the concept of using explicit disturbance information, but differs significantly by using estimated wrenches to modulate actor features while strictly maintaining symmetry, as well as explicitly training on cross-load response comparisons.

### II-B Symmetry in Humanoid Locomotion
The bilateral morphological symmetry of a robot's body serves as a powerful inductive bias. Previous work, such as SE-Policy, incorporated reflection equivariance (ensuring that mirrored observations produce mirrored action outputs) into the actor architecture, successfully stabilizing walking on physical humanoids.

However, satisfying equivariance alone does not guarantee identical velocity tracking across different loading conditions under the same command. Even an equivariant policy can exhibit load-dependent directional biases. ReACT leverages the transformation properties of disturbance wrenches to cross-condition features, achieving effective load adaptation without breaking reflection symmetry.

sections.heading: Problem setup: Inputs, outputs, and optimization targets
sections.summary: Humanoid velocity tracking is formulated as a reinforcement learning task. The actor receives a 106-dimensional observation vector (including the estimated disturbance wrench) and outputs target joint positions for 15 degrees of freedom: 12 leg joints and 3 waist joints.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
The target velocity command to track is 3-dimensional: $c_{t}=(v_{x}^{\mathrm{cmd}}, v_{y}^{\mathrm{cmd}}, \omega_{z}^{\mathrm{cmd}})$, representing forward velocity, lateral velocity, and yaw angular velocity in the robot base frame. The objective is to maintain walking stability while minimizing the absolute tracking errors $|v_{x}-v_{x}^{\mathrm{cmd}}|$, $|v_{y}-v_{y}^{\mathrm{cmd}}|$, and $|\omega_{z}-\omega_{z}^{\mathrm{cmd}}|$.

### III-B Observation and Action Spaces
- **Observation Space (Actor Input)**: Receives a 106-dimensional vector $o_{t}$. This includes the projected gravity vector, velocity commands, joint positions and velocities for the 15 controlled joints and 14 arm joints, previous whole-body action commands, and the estimated disturbance wrench $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{t}$ (forces and moments) in the torso frame. During training, the critic receives a 109-dimensional vector that additionally includes the true base linear velocity from the simulator.
- **Action Space (Actor Output)**: Outputs residual joint position targets $a_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{15}$ at 50 Hz for the 12 leg joints (6 per leg) and 3 waist joints. The 14 arm joints track externally provided trajectories and are excluded from the locomotion action space, though their states are observed by the actor.
- **Reflection Operator**: A bilateral reflection operator $F_{q}$ is defined to swap left and right corresponding joints and invert signs based on joint rotation axes.

sections.heading: Core of ReACT: Reflection-consistent modulation and cross-load consistency
sections.summary: ReACT is built on two pillars: reflection-consistent disturbance modulation, which scales and cross-couples actor features based on wrench symmetry properties, and cross-load tracking consistency training, which penalizes differences in horizontal displacement and yaw angle across unloaded, left-loaded, and right-loaded environments under identical commands.
sections.details:
### IV-A Reflection-Consistent Disturbance Modulation
When an object carried in one hand is switched to the other hand (a bilateral reflection), vertical gravity remains in the same direction, but the roll moment flips sign. ReACT decomposes the estimated disturbance wrench into a reflection-invariant symmetric component $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{sym}}=(\hat{F}_{x},\hat{F}_{z},\hat{M}_{y})$ and a sign-inverting antisymmetric component $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{asym}}=(\hat{F}_{y},\hat{M}_{x},\hat{M}_{z})$.

Inside the network, latent features extracted from wrench-free observations are split into symmetric features $h_{\mathrm{sym}}$ and antisymmetric features $h_{\mathrm{asym}}$. A modulation function $\mathcal{M}$ is then applied. Specifically, scale factors $\beta$ and coupling parameters $g$ derived from invariant information $\eta$ update the features as follows:
$h_{\mathrm{sym}}^{\prime} = h_{\mathrm{sym}} \odot [1 + \alpha \tanh(\beta_{\mathrm{sym}})] + \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{sym}}(g, h_{\mathrm{asym}})$
$h_{\mathrm{asym}}^{\prime} = h_{\mathrm{asym}} \odot [1 + \alpha \tanh(\beta_{\mathrm{asym}})] + \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{asym}}(g, h_{\mathrm{sym}})$
where $\mathcal{B}$ denotes bilinear mappings. Crucially, taking products of two antisymmetric terms yields a symmetric update term, allowing cross-branch feature coupling. This design enables the policy to differentiate between positive and negative antisymmetric disturbances (e.g., left vs. right hand loads) while strictly preserving reflection equivariance, which simple scaling cannot achieve.

### IV-B Cross-Load Tracking Consistency Training
Enforcing symmetry alone does not eliminate load-dependent tracking biases where the robot tracks accurately when unloaded but drifts laterally when loaded under the same command. To fix this, subsets of the 4096 parallel training environments are grouped into triplets: unloaded (U), left-hand loaded (L), and right-hand loaded (R).

These three environments share identical initial states and velocity commands. Over comparison windows of $T=0.4$ s, the changes in horizontal displacement and heading $\Delta\xi_{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ are recorded. A consistency reward $r^{\mathrm{con}}$ penalizes deviations from the triplet mean $\bar{\Delta\xi}$. If any environment in the triplet falls, an early-termination penalty is applied to all three. This guides the robot to follow the exact same geometric path regardless of load presence or asymmetry.

sections.heading: Validation on the physical Unitree G1: Zero collisions in autonomous navigation
sections.summary: In simulation, ReACT substantially reduced velocity errors compared to the FALCON baseline, suppressing persistent tracking biases by over an order of magnitude. In real-world mapless navigation on the Unitree G1 with a unilateral 1.5 kg load, ReACT achieved 100% collision-free goal reaching across 40 trials.
sections.details:
### V-A Implementation Details
The framework was implemented using Isaac Gym with FastSAC as the RL algorithm. An MLP-based wrench estimator was pretrained on a 15-frame proprioceptive history and frozen, passing force and moment estimates through a first-order low-pass filter (time constant $\tau=0.32$ s) to the actor. In evaluations, this estimator achieved a 100% sign agreement with ground-truth simulation wrenches.

### V-B Velocity Tracking Performance (Simulation)
Policies were evaluated under three protocols: straight walking (E1), steady turning (E2), and dynamic command changes (E3), compared against FALCON, a leading whole-body coordination baseline.
ReACT reduced forward velocity MAE by 38.8–52.9%, lateral velocity MAE by 32.0–33.5%, and yaw velocity MAE by 81.6–84.4% relative to FALCON, alongside an approximate 40% reduction in normalized torque cost. For persistent bias during straight walking, FALCON showed drift up to $0.186$ m/s laterally and $0.598$ rad/s in yaw, whereas ReACT maintained lateral drift under $0.009$ m/s and yaw drift under $0.029$ rad/s—reducing persistent biases by more than an order of magnitude.

### V-C Ablation Studies
- **Without Consistency Training (w/o Consistency)**: Yaw velocity errors surged, and lateral bias variation worsened to roughly $0.25$–$0.30$ m/s.
- **Without Modulation (w/o Modulation, replaced with standard MLP concatenation)**: The policy produced non-zero reflection residuals (0.0695 rad), breaking symmetry and causing yaw velocity error to spike to 2.7 times that of ReACT.
- **Direct Equivariant Conditioning (Equiv. Conditioning)**: Simply concatenating inputs while enforcing reflection equivariance resulted in forward velocity error roughly 4 times larger and yaw error roughly 2 times larger than ReACT, validating the bilinear modulation architecture.

### V-D Real-Robot Experiments
Using the physical Unitree G1 carrying a 1.5 kg dumbbell in one hand, autonomous mapless navigation tests were conducted in unknown environments. A frozen DRL-DCLP navigation policy provided forward and yaw velocity commands.
Across two obstacle layouts tested with both hands loaded (4 conditions, 10 runs each, 40 trials total), FALCON suffered from continuous drift, moved into obstacles, and failed in all 40 trials due to collisions. In contrast, ReACT actively counteracted unilateral load drift at the locomotion level and reached the goal without a single collision in all 40 trials (100% success rate).

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: ReACT dramatically reduces velocity tracking biases under unilateral hand loads through reflection-consistent disturbance modulation and cross-load consistency training. Its 100% success rate in physical navigation tests marks an important step toward practical humanoid transport tasks.
sections.details:
This study focused on the critical real-world problem of accumulating velocity tracking biases when humanoids carry objects in one hand, proposing ReACT as a solution.

By integrating a disturbance modulation network that strictly reflects physical symmetries with cross-load consistency training in reinforcement learning, the authors demonstrated remarkable tracking precision and robustness in simulation and on real hardware. Without modifying the frozen high-level navigation policy, simply deploying ReACT in the lower locomotion layer completely prevented collisions in physical environments—a major practical advantage for modular system integration.

Future research directions include extending the framework to scenarios where payload weight and grasp positions vary dynamically during manipulation tasks, as well as handling wider ranges of load weights and real-world velocity commands.

takeaways: Under asymmetric loads like unilateral hand carrying, the primary failure mode in navigation is not falling, but the accumulation of subtle lateral drift and yaw biases.

To combine disturbance adaptation with morphological reflection symmetry (equivariance), decomposing disturbances into symmetric and antisymmetric components and coupling them via bilinear mappings is highly effective.

Directly penalizing response differences across unloaded, left-loaded, and right-loaded conditions under identical commands (Cross-Load Consistency) plays a decisive role in eliminating tracking biases.
limitations: Experiments evaluated loads up to 4 kg in simulation and 1.5 kg on hardware; behavior under heavier extreme loads remains unverified.
Dynamic load transitions, such as picking up or placing an object midway through transport, are not addressed and remain future work.
In steady-state turning evaluations on the physical robot, while ReACT achieved low forward and yaw errors, its lateral velocity error was higher than some baselines.
